summary: For ages 11–12: understand WHY certain gases warm the planet at a molecular level. Separate the two radiations first (short-wave sunlight in, long-wave infrared out), model 'trapping' as a molecule absorbing an IR photon and re-emitting it in all directions (not a reflecting lid), contrast IR-active gases (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O — three-or-more atoms whose vibrations change the dipole moment) with IR-transparent symmetric diatomics N2/O2, distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the human-enhanced one, and compare gases by potency × abundance × lifetime. A causal photon-and-molecule investigation is proposed to lead; categorisation, dialogue, and reference diagrams consolidate. All activities are proposed, research-informed approaches whose effectiveness has not been validated.
misconceptions: Confusing the greenhouse effect with the ozone hole — believing warming is caused by holes 'letting extra heat in'. These are distinct: ozone depletion is about UV and CFCs in the stratosphere; the greenhouse effect is about IR absorption by GHGs in the troposphere.
Thinking GHGs 'reflect' heat back like a mirror or form a solid 'blanket/lid'. The real mechanism is absorption and omnidirectional re-emission of infrared by individual molecules.
Assuming the most abundant gases (nitrogen, oxygen) must be the greenhouse gases. In fact N2 and O2 are IR-transparent; the trace gases (CO2 ~0.04%, CH4 far less) do the trapping.
Believing the greenhouse effect is inherently bad. The natural effect is essential for life; the concern is the human-caused ENHANCEMENT.
Treating 'CO2 is the problem' as the whole story and ignoring methane, or conversely thinking methane's higher potency makes CO2 unimportant — missing the concentration × potency × lifetime picture.

activities.title: Photon-and-molecule energy-balance investigation
steps: Start with air made only of N2 and O2: watch the Sun emit short-wave photons that pass straight through the gas layer and warm the ground, and watch the ground re-emit red infrared photons that escape to space while a surface thermometer sits low.

Drag a few CO2 molecules into the air and observe what happens when an outgoing IR photon meets one: the molecule bends/jiggles (its bonds flexing in a mode that changes its dipole) and re-emits the photon in a random direction — roughly half the time back toward the ground.
Add more CO2 (and try CH4, H2O) and record how the surface thermometer and an 'escaping to space' counter change.
Swap the added gas for extra N2 or O2 and note that outgoing IR passes through untouched — nothing changes.

Toggle 'strip all greenhouse gases' and observe the modelled surface temperature fall toward about 255 K (−18 °C); then toggle to air containing greenhouse gases and see it rise to a habitable mean (≈ 288 K / +15 °C). The ~+33 °C jump is the NATURAL greenhouse warming; present-day air carries this natural effect plus a smaller human-enhanced increment on top. Present all figures as model outputs, not precise measurements.

In a comparison mode, match a few CH4 molecules against many CO2 molecules to feel potency per molecule versus abundance; write one sentence explaining why both a highly potent trace gas and an abundant weaker one matter. Note the comparison depends on a stated GWP time horizon.
activities.insight: Warming happens because the atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave sunlight but partly opaque to Earth's outgoing infrared: only molecules whose vibrations change their dipole moment absorb and re-emit that IR (the main greenhouse gases CO2, CH4, N2O and H2O all have three or more atoms), sending some back down and slowing heat's escape. Symmetric N2/O2 — 99% of the air — do not absorb IR, which is why trace gases dominate the effect. The natural effect is essential; human emissions enhance it.

activities.title: Two-band spectrum and molecular-vibration reference
steps: Study a two-band spectrum picture: the Sun's emission curve peaking in the visible beside Earth's emission curve peaking in the thermal IR near 10 µm, with atmospheric absorption bands shaded and the 8–15 µm window where IR escapes marked.
Use ball-and-spring molecular models to compare the symmetric stretch of O2/N2 (no dipole change → IR-transparent) with the bending and asymmetric stretch of CO2 (dipole change → IR-active).

Read GWP comparison bars showing warming per kilogram emitted over the stated time horizon (CH4 ≫ CO2) alongside atmospheric concentration (CO2 ≫ CH4), note the stated GWP time horizon, and explain in your own words why both gases matter.
Label a photon-and-molecule diagram: incoming short-wave arrows passing through, outgoing IR arrows caught by CO2/CH4 and re-emitted in all directions.
activities.insight: The asymmetry between how the atmosphere treats short-wave in and long-wave out is what produces the greenhouse effect, and it traces back to which molecular vibrations change the dipole moment. Potency and abundance are separate axes that must be combined (with lifetime) to judge a gas's overall contribution.

activities.title: 3D vibrational-mode inspector for CO2
steps: Rotate and view a CO2 molecule in three dimensions to see its vibrational modes: symmetric and asymmetric stretch (atoms moving along the molecule's straight line) and bending (which can happen in two perpendicular directions).
Identify which modes change the molecule's dipole moment (and therefore absorb IR) and which do not.
Relate what you see back to why CO2 absorbs outgoing infrared while symmetric N2/O2 do not.
activities.insight: Viewing a molecule's vibrational modes in 3D shows how its atoms move, and only modes that change the dipole moment absorb infrared — making the abstract 'dipole change' criterion concrete.

activities.title: Sort, sequence and explain: consolidating the discriminations
steps: Categorise gases as IR-active (CO2, CH4, H2O, N2O) or IR-transparent (N2, O2) and justify each placement by its molecular structure.

Put the mechanism in order: Sun → short-wave radiation → surface warms → emits infrared → infrared absorbed by GHG molecules → re-emitted in all directions → some returns to the surface → surface warms further (heat escapes to space more slowly).
Answer short questions: why do trace gases matter so much? how is the greenhouse effect different from the ozone hole? which radiation is actually trapped?
Estimate Earth's surface temperature with greenhouse gases versus with none, and explain the gap (≈ +33 °C natural effect; ≈ 255 K / −18 °C without GHGs, as modelled figures).
Distinguish the natural greenhouse effect from the enhanced effect and state what drives the enhancement (burning fossil fuels, agriculture).
activities.insight: Secure recall and discrimination of the key categories, sequence, and distinctions: IR-active vs IR-transparent, incoming vs outgoing radiation, greenhouse vs ozone, natural vs enhanced.

activities.title: Ask-the-climate-scientist dialogue to untangle misconceptions
steps: Pose the questions that puzzle you to a climate-scientist role (real teacher, peer-in-role, or a guided prompt), e.g. 'Why don't nitrogen and oxygen trap heat if they're 99% of the air?' and 'Isn't warming just the ozone hole letting heat in?'
Explain back, in your own words, why only certain molecules absorb IR and how greenhouse warming differs from ozone depletion.
Probe the follow-ups: is water vapour a human 'switch' like CO2 or a feedback? Is the greenhouse effect itself the problem, or its enhancement? What does 'potent' mean for methane?
activities.insight: Articulating and defending the mechanism through dialogue can expose and help repair the misconception-heavy areas of this topic — abundance vs IR-activity, greenhouse vs ozone, natural vs enhanced, potency vs amount.

checkQuestion: The atmosphere is nearly 99% nitrogen and oxygen, yet these gases play almost no part in the greenhouse effect, while CO₂ at under 0.05% does. Why do CO₂ and methane trap heat but nitrogen and oxygen don't — and which radiation are they actually trapping: incoming sunlight, or something else?
checkAnswer: The Sun's energy arrives mainly as short-wave radiation, which passes through; Earth's surface warms and re-emits long-wave infrared. Greenhouse-gas molecules (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) have bonds that vibrate at infrared frequencies with a changing dipole, so they absorb and re-emit that outgoing IR; symmetrical N₂ and O₂ have no dipole change when they vibrate, so they don't absorb IR. So greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared, not incoming sunlight — and it's molecular structure, not abundance, that matters.
